Can CDW Corporation Restore Margin Momentum in the Second Half?
Fri, October 2, 2026 at 4:15 AM PDT 4 min read
CDW Corporation CDW has entered the second half of 2026 with a focus on improving operating leverage and expense efficiency after delivering solid second-quarter results. The company reported second-quarter net sales of $6.6 billion, up 10% year over year, while gross profit increased 6% to $1.3 billion. Non-GAAP operating income rose 7% to $556 million, and non-GAAP earnings per share increased 12% to $2.91. However, gross margin declined 70 basis points (bps) year over year to 20.1%, reflecting a greater contribution from large hardware infrastructure opportunities related to modernization and AI readiness, particularly among enterprise customers, along with a lower relative contribution from services.
On the last earnings call, management highlighted that the gross-margin pressure was primarily a function of business mix rather than like-for-like pricing pressure. CDW maintained pricing discipline and continued to pass through price increases, while the growing mix of infrastructure products, larger-dollar orders and enterprise customers carried relatively lower margins. At the same time, netted-down revenue streams increased 16.1% and accounted for 35.9% of gross profit, up 300 bps year over year. Services grew only 1% as customers prioritized hardware and cloud investments and deployment timing affected demand, although CDW expects life-cycle and professional services activity to increase as customers move from procurement toward implementation and management.
The second half is expected to bring greater benefits from CDW's Geared for Growth initiatives. Second-quarter non-GAAP SG&A represented 57.9% of gross profit, down 20 bps year over year and 410 bps sequentially. Management said the second-quarter improvement in operating leverage largely reflected expense discipline and broader efficiency measures, while the more significant benefits from Geared for Growth are expected to emerge in the back half. The company expects both operating leverage and its expense ratio to improve sequentially through the second half and into 2027.
For 2026, CDW expects gross profit to grow in the mid-single digits, although second-half gross margins are projected to remain below year-ago levels because of product and end-market mix. Third-quarter non-GAAP SG&A is expected to decline sequentially, helping reduce operating expenses as a percentage of gross profit both year over year and sequentially. Management also expects services demand to strengthen as current infrastructure projects progress into implementation, supporting its expectation for improving operating leverage during the second half.
ServiceNow, Inc.'s NOW margins remain under pressure as rising AI adoption and greater reliance on hyperscaler infrastructure increase costs. In the second quarter of 2026, non-GAAP total gross margin declined to 78% from 81% a year earlier, while subscription gross margin fell 250 bps to 80.5%. Despite the pressure, non-GAAP operating margin remained stable at 29.5%, supported by revenue outperformance and disciplined spending. For 2026, ServiceNow continues to target an 81% non-GAAP subscription gross margin and 31.5% operating margin. Management expects AI-driven efficiencies, including roughly $500 million in internal savings, to help offset infrastructure and integration-related margin pressures.
Accenture plc's ACN margins remained relatively stable in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, despite ongoing investments in AI, talent and acquisitions. Gross margin was 32.8%, slightly below 32.9% in the year-ago quarter, reflecting continued cost pressures from its labor-intensive delivery model and evolving AI-led services. However, operating income increased 6% year over year to $3.18 billion, while operating margin expanded 20 bps to 17% from 16.8%. SG&A expenses declined to 15.8% of revenues from 16%. Strong Managed Services growth and disciplined cost management supported profitability, although AI-driven delivery changes and higher acquisition spending could influence margins going forward.
Avnet, Inc.'s AVT margin profile is improving as higher volumes, favorable mix and operating leverage support profitability. Adjusted operating margin expanded to 3.8% in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, up 73 bps sequentially and 129 bps year over year. Electronic Components margin reached 4.1%, while Farnell's margin rose to 9% from 4.3% a year earlier, supported by a higher mix of on-board components. Management expects Farnell to reach double-digit margins before the end of fiscal 2027 and consolidated SG&A as a percentage of gross profit to fall below 60%. However, gross margin remains sensitive to regional mix and pricing dynamics.

pages.title: CDW Summit 2026: IT Leaders Seek a New North Star in the Age of AI
pages.text:
CDW Summit 2026: IT Leaders Seek a New North Star in the Age of AI | FedTech Magazine
IT leaders gather to share the latest technology insights at the 2026 CDW Summit.
New Research from CDW Explores AI and Cybersecurity
Learn how AI is helping IT teams manage risk and improve resilience.
IT leaders are the midst of an identity crisis. Long seen as back-office superheroes, some IT leaders now find themselves expected to serve as innovators, evangelists and even the “fun people.”
“I didn’t know that we were the fun people, man. Like, I was supposed to do one thing, now I have to worry about if it’s fun or not?” said Carollo Engineers CIO Andrew Ivey to his fellow panelist, St. Luke’s University Health Network Associate CISO Krista Arndt.
The two were having an introspective but casual discussion about how they were responding to all of the changes in the workplace and IT — especially those wrought by artificial intelligence.
But the setup for this conference conversation was different. The panel, which took place onstage during the 2026 CDW Summit in Dallas, had a podcast aesthetic to it and it was dubbed “CDW OTR (On the Record).” The two had big podcast mics in front of them, and Arndt was dressed more casually and sitting cross-legged on the couch. This could have been a conversation livestreaming from YouTube or Twitch.
Click the banner below to learn how organizations are unlocking artificial intelligence’s potential.
The idea that IT leaders would present themselves in such a down-to-earth manner would have seemed out of place more than five years ago. But this change in tone and style is a sign of the times. And the idea that it’s important to infuse fun, excitement or positivity into their IT management styles was one that Arndt clearly embraced more easily than Ivey, who viewed his role as an IT leader as more of an honest broker and a skeptic — especially when it comes to the AI hype cycle.
“I think it’s your responsibility to be the voice of reason and to help guide this. And if you don’t have a skeptic in the room, then guess what your job is: to be the skeptic,” said Ivey. “If you have a skeptic in the room, then it’s probably not helpful for you also to be a skeptic. But you need one. And so, go find one, bring them in the room, just so they can poke holes in this thing early on. And I think you’ll survive and build a bulletproof project if you just bring in a naysayer early.”
Arndt said she prioritizes a highly collaborative but honest and authentic approach to IT leadership. For her, having a positive relationship and effective communication with her non-IT counterparts is critical to her role as a security leader.
“Our technology organization has a phenomenal relationship with our hospital leadership, and they talk constantly,” said Arndt. “It’s something that we focus on a lot in security: speaking the language of people that we serve so they really understand what’s going on.”
Those conversations, which might seem more casual than they were in the past, are extremely valuable in Arndt’s pursuit of getting her non-IT counterparts to receive her concerns about risk management.
“Having those open conversations where you can just be yourself and feel like you’re not just trying to put on a show for your leadership … I do see that happening,” added Arndt. “They know there’s a lot of unknowns, but they’re really excited to investigate those reasonably and from a risk-balance basis.”
DISCOVER: How to optimize your agency's infrastructure for artificial intelligence.
Linking AI With Strategic Business Imperatives
As she walked out to the main stage to welcome the more than 600 attendees at the Sheraton Dallas Hotel, CDW Chief Commercial Officer Liz Connelly acknowledged that everyone in tech has been talking a lot about AI, and that many people are eager for the next step.
“OK, we know you’ve heard a lot about AI,” said Connelly. “We won’t be spending time simply admiring the opportunities and challenges around AI. We’ll be sharing our well-informed point of view on what to prioritize, what to build and what to do next. Because the question is no longer whether AI will change business. The question is how organizations can use AI to deliver real and measurable business ambition outcomes.”
To highlight just how CDW was putting its money where its mouth is, Connelly brought out the company’s recently hired chief strategy and transformation officer, Hang Tan.
Tan, who has been tasked with advancing CDW’s AI strategy, highlighted how CDW has decided to treat itself as “Customer Zero” as it deploys and learns from its own AI implementations.
CDW Chief Strategy and Transformation Officer Hang Tan speaks about CDW’s six AI imperatives, which are informed by its “Customer Zero” approach to AI, at the 2026 CDW Summit.
During his presentation, Tan shared six core AI imperatives that CDW has developed that he believes can also help guide its customers’ thinking around AI:
AI-ready infrastructure: “This is more than just securing GPU capacity, because when we're when we're talking about agents, agents will put entirely new demands across all of your infrastructure — your public cloud, your data center, your network, and your endpoints.”
Getting your data ready for AI: “This is all about giving AI secure access to your unique business context. But then, once you do that, your AI will start to generate data. How do you manage the AI-generated data, and how do you extract insights from that data?”
Activating AI in existing software platforms: “As these platforms introduce new agentic capabilities, you have a very tricky or important set of decisions to make: Where does it make sense to activate AI within each of your platforms, but where does it make sense to actually develop AI capabilities on top and across your platforms?”
Adopting assistants and agentic platforms. “Everybody here in the room are well down the path of adopting AI assistants, but the magic really happens when you move past the, ‘Hey, let's give everybody Copilot and have them experiment on their own,’ to how do you get to shared learning, shared experimentation, shared skills, shared agents? That’s where the benefit, the productivity, will really scale.”
Security: “How do you evolve your identity and your security controls to extend beyond just users, devices, but to also extend to agents?”
Financial discipline around AI: “It’s more than just tracking what the spend is or controlling the spend because, remember, if you really want to demonstrate business outcomes, you need to instrument both the AI, but also instrument your processes.”
The tone that CDW’s leadership was taking with AI was clear and focused on outcomes, and a sign that IT is intent on getting to a place of real progress when it comes to AI. The tech industry has spent a lot of time talking about how AI will change things, but many in IT are eager to see more proof of this change — and not just doomsday warnings or the frothy hype.
Humanoid Robotics Is Funny Stuff, but Also Serious Business
As Arndt and Ivey debated the state of IT and how drastically AI will reshape their industry, CDW Senior Vice President of Vertical Markets Mike Grisamore interrupted their conversation to bring out a special guest: CDW’s own humanoid robot, named CH3T.
The robot actually made its debut six months earlier, at the 2026 HIMSS Global Health Conference & Exhibition in Las Vegas. Nonetheless, the robot was an instant favorite with the audience at the Summit as it teetered out onto the stage wearing scrub pants and a Team USA hat, a nod to CDW’s role as an official sponsor of the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles.
CH3T comes out on stage to hang out with CDW’s panelists and moderators during the CDW OTR mainstage event at the 2026 CDW Summit.
“CH3T, by the way, those are some sweet scrubs you got,” teased Grisamore. “Apparently, when CH3T first joined us, CH3T came out, and having CH3T without pants on was a little disturbing to some of the nurses. So, CH3T now has scrubs, which are pretty sweet. And I know normally you wear your Crocs, like every good clinician does, but I do like the CDW red.”
While the bit between CH3T and the hosts was fun, and audience members seemed to marvel at the technical prowess of a robot that walked and responded to human interaction in real time, Grisamore noted that despite the lighthearted banter between him and the humanoid robot, CH3T was more than entertainment. He represented a meaningful investment on the part of CDW in promise of physical AI.
“We think about physical AI, and looking at them just as platforms, because we know that investing kind of in what’s next, it doesn’t always fit into everyone’s immediate budget,” said Grisamore. “Not that we have a massive budget to do it, but the opportunity to carve out a little bit and start thinking about, ‘All right, how do we take CH3T, or, you know, two generations past CH3T, and start thinking about, ‘All right, what are the use cases where there is a return on investment?’”
“We’ve got one of CH3T’s brothers that is pushing wheelchairs around, and we’re thinking about transport. We’re thinking about utilization, because CH3T, when he’s not pushing someone around in a wheelchair, he could be going and restocking supply closets,” added Grisamore.
Maybe CH3T is proof that IT can be about a little bit of fun and a little bit of business at the same time. And that IT is in a place where it can do more, be more and achieve more than it ever has in the past.

CDW's Buyback Pace Jumps: Can Stronger Cash Flow Sustain Returns?
Wed, September 30, 2026 at 5:59 AM PDT 3 min read
CDW Corporation CDW has stepped up capital returns in 2026, with share repurchases gaining notable momentum even as free cash flow (FCF) conversion remained below its historical framework during the first half. In the second quarter, the company returned $344 million to shareholders through buybacks and another $80 million through dividends.
First-half repurchases totaled approximately $545 million, already approaching the $653 million deployed during all of 2025 and exceeding the $500 million repurchased in each of 2023 and 2024. Including dividends, CDW returned $706 million to shareholders during the first half of 2026. The company also added $1 billion to its share repurchase authorization during the quarter, leaving more than $1.1 billion of remaining capacity and providing considerable flexibility for further buybacks.
The sustainability of this faster capital-return pace will partly depend on a recovery in cash generation. Adjusted free cash flow was $278 million in the first half, representing 42% of non-GAAP net income and falling below management's long-term rule of thumb of converting 80-90% of non-GAAP net income into cash.
On the last earnings call, management attributed the shortfall primarily to working-capital timing as CDW invested to support hardware-driven growth and customer demand amid elevated pricing. Inventory increased by roughly $400 million from year-end, but management expects to rationalize inventory as supply conditions become more normalized, making inventory reduction the biggest variable behind an anticipated improvement in second-half free cash flow.
CDW's balance sheet also provides some support for continued shareholder distributions. Net leverage ended the quarter at 2.5X, comfortably within management's 2X-3X target range, while liquidity was $2 billion. The company continues to target a dividend payout of roughly 25% of non-GAAP net income and remains active in evaluating acquisitions that broaden its capabilities and customer relevance.
Meanwhile, Geared for Growth initiatives are expected to improve expense efficiency and operating leverage during the second half and into 2027, potentially strengthening future investment and capital-deployment capacity.
ServiceNow NOW generated $2.257 billion of operating cash flow in the first half of 2026 and continues to target a 35% FCF margin for 2026. The company also expects around $500 million in internal AI efficiency savings this year, supporting cash generation while keeping headcount flat despite acquisitions. TTM cash flow conversion is 317.8%, above its 276.5% median, while FCF conversion is 274.3%, also above its 242.4% median. Strong cash conversion supports reinvestment and acquisition funding. However, the company's cash flow includes substantial stock-based compensation and acquisition spending, which should be monitored.
Accenture plc ACN continues to generate strong cash flow while returning capital to shareholders. In the fiscal third quarter of 2026, operating cash flow rose to $3.79 billion, while free cash flow increased to $3.60 billion. The company repurchased or redeemed 6 million shares for $1.2 billion and paid $1 billion in dividends, or $1.63 per share, reflecting a 10% increase. Accenture ended the quarter with $10.2 billion in cash, while $3.2 billion remained under its share repurchase authorization. For fiscal 2026, operating cash flow is expected at $11.5-$12.2 billion and FCF at $10.8-$11.5 billion.

CDW's $525M Lovelytics Buyout: Can Data & AI Services Boost Growth?
A key trend shaping enterprise technology currently is the growing need to turn AI experimentation into measurable business value. CDW Corporation CDW is making a sizable bet on this booming demand. The company recently announced plans to acquire Lovelytics, a data and AI services firm and member of the Databricks Brickbuilder Partner Network, for approximately $525 million. Expected to close in the third quarter, the transaction is designed to strengthen CDW's Data & Analytics Practice and expand its broader Services & Solutions portfolio.
By adding Lovelytics' specialized data, analytics and AI expertise to its extensive technology portfolio and customer base, CDW aims to position itself as a more comprehensive partner for enterprises moving from AI pilots to production. According to Gartner research cited by CDW, only 12% of enterprises feel fully prepared for AI data readiness. That gap creates a huge opportunity for technology service providers capable of helping organizations modernize fragmented data environments, establish governance and build architectures suitable for AI. Enterprises need clean, accessible data, modern analytics platforms, appropriate governance and security, and increasingly sophisticated AI applications. This is precisely where Lovelytics fits into CDW's strategy.
CDW continues to supplement organic growth through acquisitions while maintaining shareholder-return commitments and operational discipline. Prior acquisitions such as Mission Cloud Services, Enquizit, Sirius Computer Solutions and Lexicon Tech Solutions expanded cloud, managed services and lifecycle capabilities that support current customer priorities. If CDW successfully combines Lovelytics' specialized expertise with its scale, customer relationships and broad technology portfolio, the acquisition is likely to become a major growth engine for its Services & Solutions business.
Competition Heats Up for CDW in Enterprise AI
ServiceNow's NOW acquisitions of Moveworks, Armis and Veza broaden its reach across employee workflows, cybersecurity and identity governance. In August 2026, management said Armis and Veza exceeded their plans in the first quarter under NOW and pulled demand into the core security and risk, CMDB and ITOM businesses. As of August 2026, management said the CRM business had surpassed $2 billion. Combining asset intelligence, identity governance and AI Control Tower enables customers to detect, assess and remediate security issues on one platform. This supports cross-selling into established workflows and aligns with customer demand for security, risk and governance as AI deployment expands.
Accenture plc ACN has a disciplined acquisition strategy focused on adding skills in high-growth areas and deepening industry expertise. It spent $1.5 billion across 23 strategic acquisitions in fiscal 2025. In the fiscal third quarter, management said it invested about $3 billion primarily across 13 acquisitions year to date and expected roughly $9 billion of fiscal 2026 buyout investment, assuming announced transactions close. In August, Accenture agreed to acquire Dutch SAP specialist McCoy, adding more than 380 professionals and boosting SAP modernization and AI capabilities for European mid-market clients. Accenture's acquisition program is becoming more capital intensive, with management expecting roughly $9 billion of fiscal 2026 investment.

Is the Options Market Predicting a Spike in CDW Stock?
Tue, September 29, 2026 at 7:13 AM PDT 2 min read
Investors in CDW, Inc. CDW need to pay close attention to the stock based on moves in the options market lately. That is because the October 16, 2026 $175.00 Put had some of the highest implied volatility of all equity options today.
What is Implied Volatility?
Implied volatility shows how much movement the market is expecting in the future. Options with high levels of implied volatility suggest that investors in the underlying stocks are expecting a big move in one direction or the other. It could also mean there is an event coming up soon that may cause a big rally or a huge sell off. However, implied volatility is only one piece of the puzzle when putting together an options trading strategy.
What do the Analysts Think?
Clearly, options traders are pricing in a big move for CDW, but what is the fundamental picture for the company? Currently, CDW is a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) in the Computers - IT Services Industry that ranks in the Top 27% of our Zacks Industry Rank. Over the last 60 days, three analysts have increased their estimates for the current quarter, while one has revised his estimate downward. The net effect has taken our Zacks Consensus Estimate for the current quarter to move from $2.91 per share to $2.92 per share in the same time period.
Given the way analysts feel about CDW right now, this huge implied volatility could mean there's a trade developing. Often times, options traders look for options with high levels of implied volatility to sell premium. This is a strategy many seasoned traders use because it captures decay. At expiration, the hope for these traders is that the underlying stock does not move as much as originally expected.

pages.title: CDW Canada’s AI Workplace Trends Report Finds Canadian Organizations Entering New Phase of AI Maturity as Agentic AI Gains Ground

CDW Canada’s AI Workplace Trends Report Finds Canadian Organizations Entering New Phase of AI Maturity as Agentic AI Gains Ground
New research shows AI is moving beyond experimentation in Canadian workplaces, but trust, training and measurement remain critical barriers to realizing business outcomes.
ETOBICOKE, Ontario, September 22, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Today, CDW Canada, the strategic end-to-end technology partner that turns customer ambition into outcomes, released new research exploring how Canadian organizations are moving from artificial intelligence (AI) deployment to realizing business value. The report, Canada's AI Workplace Evolution from Adoption to Accountability, draws on a survey conducted by Earnscliffe on behalf of CDW Canada of 1,011 Canadian office workers across organizations of varying sizes and industries throughout Canada.
The report finds AI is now firmly embedded in Canadian workplaces, with daily use of workplace-approved AI tools nearly doubling year over year (31 percent, up from 18 percent). But as adoption becomes mainstream, organizations are increasingly focused on a more pressing challenge: turning AI investments into measurable business outcomes. The research also points to the rapid rise of agentic AI, with one third of employees already reporting the use of AI agents capable of completing multistep workflows, making recommendations and helping drive outcomes.
"AI adoption is no longer the story," said KJ Burke, Field CTO, Hybrid Infrastructure, CDW Canada. "Most organizations have moved beyond asking whether employees will use AI. The question now is whether those investments are creating meaningful business value. The organizations that lead in the years ahead will be the ones that can measure impact, build trust and reimagine how work gets done by empowering employees to work effectively with AI systems."
The next phase of workplace AI is already taking shape, signalling a shift from AI tools that assist with individual tasks to systems that can help execute more complex workflows and contribute to outcomes.
The research suggests organizations are beginning to move from simply consuming AI technologies to actively shaping them. Nearly one-in-three agentic AI users report their organization is already building AI agents in-house.
At the same time, the findings highlight the importance of employee enablement. Workers who receive hands-on AI training report significantly higher levels of confidence using AI (46 percent are very confident) than those who receive no formal support (23 percent), underscoring the growing need for practical, role-specific training as AI capabilities become more advanced.
"Agentic AI represents an important shift in how organizations think about AI," said KJ Burke, Field CTO, Hybrid Infrastructure, CDW Canada. "As AI evolves from assisting employees to helping execute work, organizations must invest not only in technology, but also in the skills, governance and trust required to use it responsibly and effectively."
Trust remains the biggest obstacle to deeper AI adoption
Employee attitudes toward AI continue to trend positively. Curiosity remains the dominant sentiment among workers (42 percent) and outweighs the percentage that are worried about AI, suggesting employees are increasingly open to AI in the workplace.
However, trust continues to be a barrier to broader and deeper adoption. Accuracy and reliability are among the top AI concerns across daily users (31 percent), less frequent users (24 percent) and those not yet using approved tools (43 percent).
The findings also show that barriers vary depending on an employee's experience with AI. More advanced users tend to focus on privacy and security concerns, while those who have yet to embrace AI are more likely to question both its reliability and its relevance to their role.
"The challenge for organizations is no longer generating interest in AI," said Ashley Otto, Senior Product Manager, CDW Canada. "It's helping employees trust the technology enough to use it confidently and effectively. That requires clear governance, practical use cases and ongoing education."
Organizations are beginning to see value, but many still struggle to measure it
The research suggests AI is delivering benefits beyond simple efficiency gains. Compared to 2025, employees with access to AI at work increasingly report improvements in productivity (58 percent, up 11 points), quality of outputs (54 percent, up 15 points) and innovation (48 percent, up 11 points), indicating that organizations are beginning to realize broader business value from AI investments.
Despite this progress, many organizations continue to face a measurement gap. While more organizations report tracking specific KPIs to evaluate AI performance than they did a year ago (38 percent, up from 24 percent), a significant number still lack formal frameworks to assess ROI (23 percent) or are unsure whether such measurement exists (23 percent).
As AI programs mature and investment scrutiny intensifies, the ability to measure and communicate impact is critical to ensuring effective adoption. For CDW Canada, that means helping organizations move beyond AI implementation to building sustainable programs grounded in strategy, employee enablement, governance and measurable business outcomes.
"Most organizations can tell you how many employees have access to AI," said Burke. "Far fewer can clearly demonstrate what AI has changed for their business. We're entering an accountability phase where success will be defined not by access or experimentation, but by an organization's ability to prove value and sustain results."
For Canadian organizations, the next phase of AI success will be defined by trust, workforce readiness and measurable outcomes. As organizations explore emerging technologies such as agentic AI, CDW Canada is helping customers build the strategies, skills and governance frameworks needed to turn AI investments into lasting business value.
To learn more about the state of AI in Canadian workplaces, download the full 2026 Canadian AI Workspace Trends Report: Canada's AI Workplace Evolution from Adoption to Accountability.
Join the conversation online by following @CDWCanada on X and LinkedIn.

The online survey was in field from June 15 to 25, 2026, with a sample of 1,011 Canadian office workers who work in organizations with at least 20 employees and use a computer in an office setting 11 or more hours a week, using Leger's LEO panel. Quotas were set for business size, sector, region, age and gender to align with sample structure from previous waves, and data is unweighted.
The survey was conducted in English. Online surveys cannot be assigned a margin of error.

Can CDW Corporation Restore Margin Momentum in the Second Half?
Fri, October 2, 2026 at 4:15 AM PDT 4 min read
CDW Corporation CDW has entered the second half of 2026 with a focus on improving operating leverage and expense efficiency after delivering solid second-quarter results. The company reported second-quarter net sales of $6.6 billion, up 10% year over year, while gross profit increased 6% to $1.3 billion. Non-GAAP operating income rose 7% to $556 million, and non-GAAP earnings per share increased 12% to $2.91. However, gross margin declined 70 basis points (bps) year over year to 20.1%, reflecting a greater contribution from large hardware infrastructure opportunities related to modernization and AI readiness, particularly among enterprise customers, along with a lower relative contribution from services.
On the last earnings call, management highlighted that the gross-margin pressure was primarily a function of business mix rather than like-for-like pricing pressure. CDW maintained pricing discipline and continued to pass through price increases, while the growing mix of infrastructure products, larger-dollar orders and enterprise customers carried relatively lower margins. At the same time, netted-down revenue streams increased 16.1% and accounted for 35.9% of gross profit, up 300 bps year over year. Services grew only 1% as customers prioritized hardware and cloud investments and deployment timing affected demand, although CDW expects life-cycle and professional services activity to increase as customers move from procurement toward implementation and management.
The second half is expected to bring greater benefits from CDW's Geared for Growth initiatives. Second-quarter non-GAAP SG&A represented 57.9% of gross profit, down 20 bps year over year and 410 bps sequentially. Management said the second-quarter improvement in operating leverage largely reflected expense discipline and broader efficiency measures, while the more significant benefits from Geared for Growth are expected to emerge in the back half. The company expects both operating leverage and its expense ratio to improve sequentially through the second half and into 2027.
For 2026, CDW expects gross profit to grow in the mid-single digits, although second-half gross margins are projected to remain below year-ago levels because of product and end-market mix. Third-quarter non-GAAP SG&A is expected to decline sequentially, helping reduce operating expenses as a percentage of gross profit both year over year and sequentially. Management also expects services demand to strengthen as current infrastructure projects progress into implementation, supporting its expectation for improving operating leverage during the second half.
ServiceNow, Inc.'s NOW margins remain under pressure as rising AI adoption and greater reliance on hyperscaler infrastructure increase costs. In the second quarter of 2026, non-GAAP total gross margin declined to 78% from 81% a year earlier, while subscription gross margin fell 250 bps to 80.5%. Despite the pressure, non-GAAP operating margin remained stable at 29.5%, supported by revenue outperformance and disciplined spending. For 2026, ServiceNow continues to target an 81% non-GAAP subscription gross margin and 31.5% operating margin. Management expects AI-driven efficiencies, including roughly $500 million in internal savings, to help offset infrastructure and integration-related margin pressures.
Accenture plc's ACN margins remained relatively stable in the third quarter of fiscal 2026, despite ongoing investments in AI, talent and acquisitions. Gross margin was 32.8%, slightly below 32.9% in the year-ago quarter, reflecting continued cost pressures from its labor-intensive delivery model and evolving AI-led services. However, operating income increased 6% year over year to $3.18 billion, while operating margin expanded 20 bps to 17% from 16.8%. SG&A expenses declined to 15.8% of revenues from 16%. Strong Managed Services growth and disciplined cost management supported profitability, although AI-driven delivery changes and higher acquisition spending could influence margins going forward.
Avnet, Inc.'s AVT margin profile is improving as higher volumes, favorable mix and operating leverage support profitability. Adjusted operating margin expanded to 3.8% in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, up 73 bps sequentially and 129 bps year over year. Electronic Components margin reached 4.1%, while Farnell's margin rose to 9% from 4.3% a year earlier, supported by a higher mix of on-board components. Management expects Farnell to reach double-digit margins before the end of fiscal 2027 and consolidated SG&A as a percentage of gross profit to fall below 60%. However, gross margin remains sensitive to regional mix and pricing dynamics.

IT leaders are the midst of an identity crisis. Long seen as back-office superheroes, some IT leaders now find themselves expected to serve as innovators, evangelists and even the “fun people.”
“I didn’t know that we were the fun people, man. Like, I was supposed to do one thing, now I have to worry about if it’s fun or not?” said Carollo Engineers CIO Andrew Ivey to his fellow panelist, St. Luke’s University Health Network Associate CISO Krista Arndt.
The two were having an introspective but casual discussion about how they were responding to all of the changes in the workplace and IT — especially those wrought by artificial intelligence.
But the setup for this conference conversation was different. The panel, which took place onstage during the 2026 CDW Summit in Dallas, had a podcast aesthetic to it and it was dubbed “CDW OTR (On the Record).” The two had big podcast mics in front of them, and Arndt was dressed more casually and sitting cross-legged on the couch. This could have been a conversation livestreaming from YouTube or Twitch.

The idea that IT leaders would present themselves in such a down-to-earth manner would have seemed out of place more than five years ago. But this change in tone and style is a sign of the times. And the idea that it’s important to infuse fun, excitement or positivity into their IT management styles was one that Arndt clearly embraced more easily than Ivey, who viewed his role as an IT leader as more of an honest broker and a skeptic — especially when it comes to the AI hype cycle.
“I think it’s your responsibility to be the voice of reason and to help guide this. And if you don’t have a skeptic in the room, then guess what your job is: to be the skeptic,” said Ivey. “If you have a skeptic in the room, then it’s probably not helpful for you also to be a skeptic. But you need one. And so, go find one, bring them in the room, just so they can poke holes in this thing early on. And I think you’ll survive and build a bulletproof project if you just bring in a naysayer early.”
Arndt said she prioritizes a highly collaborative but honest and authentic approach to IT leadership. For her, having a positive relationship and effective communication with her non-IT counterparts is critical to her role as a security leader.
“Our technology organization has a phenomenal relationship with our hospital leadership, and they talk constantly,” said Arndt. “It’s something that we focus on a lot in security: speaking the language of people that we serve so they really understand what’s going on.”
Those conversations, which might seem more casual than they were in the past, are extremely valuable in Arndt’s pursuit of getting her non-IT counterparts to receive her concerns about risk management.
“Having those open conversations where you can just be yourself and feel like you’re not just trying to put on a show for your leadership … I do see that happening,” added Arndt. “They know there’s a lot of unknowns, but they’re really excited to investigate those reasonably and from a risk-balance basis.”

Linking AI With Strategic Business Imperatives
As she walked out to the main stage to welcome the more than 600 attendees at the Sheraton Dallas Hotel, CDW Chief Commercial Officer Liz Connelly acknowledged that everyone in tech has been talking a lot about AI, and that many people are eager for the next step.
“OK, we know you’ve heard a lot about AI,” said Connelly. “We won’t be spending time simply admiring the opportunities and challenges around AI. We’ll be sharing our well-informed point of view on what to prioritize, what to build and what to do next. Because the question is no longer whether AI will change business. The question is how organizations can use AI to deliver real and measurable business ambition outcomes.”
To highlight just how CDW was putting its money where its mouth is, Connelly brought out the company’s recently hired chief strategy and transformation officer, Hang Tan.
Tan, who has been tasked with advancing CDW’s AI strategy, highlighted how CDW has decided to treat itself as “Customer Zero” as it deploys and learns from its own AI implementations.
CDW Chief Strategy and Transformation Officer Hang Tan speaks about CDW’s six AI imperatives, which are informed by its “Customer Zero” approach to AI, at the 2026 CDW Summit.
During his presentation, Tan shared six core AI imperatives that CDW has developed that he believes can also help guide its customers’ thinking around AI:
AI-ready infrastructure: “This is more than just securing GPU capacity, because when we're when we're talking about agents, agents will put entirely new demands across all of your infrastructure — your public cloud, your data center, your network, and your endpoints.”
Getting your data ready for AI: “This is all about giving AI secure access to your unique business context. But then, once you do that, your AI will start to generate data. How do you manage the AI-generated data, and how do you extract insights from that data?”
Activating AI in existing software platforms: “As these platforms introduce new agentic capabilities, you have a very tricky or important set of decisions to make: Where does it make sense to activate AI within each of your platforms, but where does it make sense to actually develop AI capabilities on top and across your platforms?”
Adopting assistants and agentic platforms. “Everybody here in the room are well down the path of adopting AI assistants, but the magic really happens when you move past the, ‘Hey, let's give everybody Copilot and have them experiment on their own,’ to how do you get to shared learning, shared experimentation, shared skills, shared agents? That’s where the benefit, the productivity, will really scale.”
Security: “How do you evolve your identity and your security controls to extend beyond just users, devices, but to also extend to agents?”
Financial discipline around AI: “It’s more than just tracking what the spend is or controlling the spend because, remember, if you really want to demonstrate business outcomes, you need to instrument both the AI, but also instrument your processes.”
The tone that CDW’s leadership was taking with AI was clear and focused on outcomes, and a sign that IT is intent on getting to a place of real progress when it comes to AI. The tech industry has spent a lot of time talking about how AI will change things, but many in IT are eager to see more proof of this change — and not just doomsday warnings or the frothy hype.
Humanoid Robotics Is Funny Stuff, but Also Serious Business
As Arndt and Ivey debated the state of IT and how drastically AI will reshape their industry, CDW Senior Vice President of Vertical Markets Mike Grisamore interrupted their conversation to bring out a special guest: CDW’s own humanoid robot, named CH3T.
The robot actually made its debut six months earlier, at the 2026 HIMSS Global Health Conference & Exhibition in Las Vegas. Nonetheless, the robot was an instant favorite with the audience at the Summit as it teetered out onto the stage wearing scrub pants and a Team USA hat, a nod to CDW’s role as an official sponsor of the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles.
CH3T comes out on stage to hang out with CDW’s panelists and moderators during the CDW OTR mainstage event at the 2026 CDW Summit.
“CH3T, by the way, those are some sweet scrubs you got,” teased Grisamore. “Apparently, when CH3T first joined us, CH3T came out, and having CH3T without pants on was a little disturbing to some of the nurses. So, CH3T now has scrubs, which are pretty sweet. And I know normally you wear your Crocs, like every good clinician does, but I do like the CDW red.”
While the bit between CH3T and the hosts was fun, and audience members seemed to marvel at the technical prowess of a robot that walked and responded to human interaction in real time, Grisamore noted that despite the lighthearted banter between him and the humanoid robot, CH3T was more than entertainment. He represented a meaningful investment on the part of CDW in promise of physical AI.
“We think about physical AI, and looking at them just as platforms, because we know that investing kind of in what’s next, it doesn’t always fit into everyone’s immediate budget,” said Grisamore. “Not that we have a massive budget to do it, but the opportunity to carve out a little bit and start thinking about, ‘All right, how do we take CH3T, or, you know, two generations past CH3T, and start thinking about, ‘All right, what are the use cases where there is a return on investment?’”
“We’ve got one of CH3T’s brothers that is pushing wheelchairs around, and we’re thinking about transport. We’re thinking about utilization, because CH3T, when he’s not pushing someone around in a wheelchair, he could be going and restocking supply closets,” added Grisamore.
Maybe CH3T is proof that IT can be about a little bit of fun and a little bit of business at the same time. And that IT is in a place where it can do more, be more and achieve more than it ever has in the past.

CDW Canada’s AI Workplace Trends Report Finds Canadian Organizations Entering New Phase of AI Maturity as Agentic AI Gains Ground
New research shows AI is moving beyond experimentation in Canadian workplaces, but trust, training and measurement remain critical barriers to realizing business outcomes.
ETOBICOKE, Ontario, September 22, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Today, CDW Canada, the strategic end-to-end technology partner that turns customer ambition into outcomes, released new research exploring how Canadian organizations are moving from artificial intelligence (AI) deployment to realizing business value. The report, Canada's AI Workplace Evolution from Adoption to Accountability, draws on a survey conducted by Earnscliffe on behalf of CDW Canada of 1,011 Canadian office workers across organizations of varying sizes and industries throughout Canada.
The report finds AI is now firmly embedded in Canadian workplaces, with daily use of workplace-approved AI tools nearly doubling year over year (31 percent, up from 18 percent). But as adoption becomes mainstream, organizations are increasingly focused on a more pressing challenge: turning AI investments into measurable business outcomes. The research also points to the rapid rise of agentic AI, with one third of employees already reporting the use of AI agents capable of completing multistep workflows, making recommendations and helping drive outcomes.
"AI adoption is no longer the story," said KJ Burke, Field CTO, Hybrid Infrastructure, CDW Canada. "Most organizations have moved beyond asking whether employees will use AI. The question now is whether those investments are creating meaningful business value. The organizations that lead in the years ahead will be the ones that can measure impact, build trust and reimagine how work gets done by empowering employees to work effectively with AI systems."
The next phase of workplace AI is already taking shape, signalling a shift from AI tools that assist with individual tasks to systems that can help execute more complex workflows and contribute to outcomes.
The research suggests organizations are beginning to move from simply consuming AI technologies to actively shaping them. Nearly one-in-three agentic AI users report their organization is already building AI agents in-house.
At the same time, the findings highlight the importance of employee enablement. Workers who receive hands-on AI training report significantly higher levels of confidence using AI (46 percent are very confident) than those who receive no formal support (23 percent), underscoring the growing need for practical, role-specific training as AI capabilities become more advanced.
"Agentic AI represents an important shift in how organizations think about AI," said KJ Burke, Field CTO, Hybrid Infrastructure, CDW Canada. "As AI evolves from assisting employees to helping execute work, organizations must invest not only in technology, but also in the skills, governance and trust required to use it responsibly and effectively."
Trust remains the biggest obstacle to deeper AI adoption
Employee attitudes toward AI continue to trend positively. Curiosity remains the dominant sentiment among workers (42 percent) and outweighs the percentage that are worried about AI, suggesting employees are increasingly open to AI in the workplace.
However, trust continues to be a barrier to broader and deeper adoption. Accuracy and reliability are among the top AI concerns across daily users (31 percent), less frequent users (24 percent) and those not yet using approved tools (43 percent).
The findings also show that barriers vary depending on an employee's experience with AI. More advanced users tend to focus on privacy and security concerns, while those who have yet to embrace AI are more likely to question both its reliability and its relevance to their role.
"The challenge for organizations is no longer generating interest in AI," said Ashley Otto, Senior Product Manager, CDW Canada. "It's helping employees trust the technology enough to use it confidently and effectively. That requires clear governance, practical use cases and ongoing education."
Organizations are beginning to see value, but many still struggle to measure it
The research suggests AI is delivering benefits beyond simple efficiency gains. Compared to 2025, employees with access to AI at work increasingly report improvements in productivity (58 percent, up 11 points), quality of outputs (54 percent, up 15 points) and innovation (48 percent, up 11 points), indicating that organizations are beginning to realize broader business value from AI investments.
Despite this progress, many organizations continue to face a measurement gap. While more organizations report tracking specific KPIs to evaluate AI performance than they did a year ago (38 percent, up from 24 percent), a significant number still lack formal frameworks to assess ROI (23 percent) or are unsure whether such measurement exists (23 percent).
As AI programs mature and investment scrutiny intensifies, the ability to measure and communicate impact is critical to ensuring effective adoption. For CDW Canada, that means helping organizations move beyond AI implementation to building sustainable programs grounded in strategy, employee enablement, governance and measurable business outcomes.
"Most organizations can tell you how many employees have access to AI," said Burke. "Far fewer can clearly demonstrate what AI has changed for their business. We're entering an accountability phase where success will be defined not by access or experimentation, but by an organization's ability to prove value and sustain results."
For Canadian organizations, the next phase of AI success will be defined by trust, workforce readiness and measurable outcomes. As organizations explore emerging technologies such as agentic AI, CDW Canada is helping customers build the strategies, skills and governance frameworks needed to turn AI investments into lasting business value.
